faqs.a: polygon() takes a list of x/y point pairs that the browser connects in order to form the clipping region. Points use percentages of the element's own width and height, so polygon(50% 0%, 0% 100%, 100% 100%) draws a triangle: top-center, bottom-left, bottom-right. Everything outside the polygon is clipped away.

clip-path clips the element's rendered box — backgrounds, borders, and content all get cut to the shape. If you want a visible border around a clipped shape, use filter: drop-shadow() instead of box-shadow, because drop-shadow follows the clipped outline while box-shadow is clipped away with the box.
faqs.q: Why does my border disappear when I apply clip-path?

faqs.a: The classic hexagon points are: 25% 0%, 75% 0%, 100% 50%, 75% 100%, 25% 100%, 0% 50%. These give flat top and bottom edges with pointed left and right sides. Rotate the point order by 90 degrees (starting at 50% 0%) for a pointy-top hexagon instead.
faqs.q: What are the polygon points for a hexagon?

faqs.a: Yes — the star preset here is a single five-pointed star drawn with ten polygon points (five outer tips, five inner valleys). Multi-star patterns need either several elements or an SVG, but one star per element is a single line of CSS.
faqs.q: Can I make a star with clip-path?

faqs.a: Mostly yes: polygon(), circle(), ellipse(), and inset() are supported in all modern browsers. The older url() form referencing SVG clipPath elements has spottier support. Stick to the basic shapes this tool generates and you are safe everywhere modern.
faqs.q: Is clip-path supported in all browsers?

faqs.a: Clipping is purely visual — the element still occupies its original rectangular box in the layout, and screen readers still see the full content. Do not use clip-path to hide sensitive content, and keep enough visible text for the shape to make sense to all users.
faqs.q: Does clip-path affect accessibility or layout?

css-clip-path-generator.formula:
clip-path: polygon(<x1> <y1>, <x2> <y2>, <x3> <y3>, ...);

Points are % of the element's width (x) and height (y), connected in order.
clip-path: circle(50% at 50% 50%);     /* perfect circle */
clip-path: ellipse(50% 35% at 50% 50%); /* wide ellipse */
clip-path: inset(10% 20% round 8px);    /* rounded inner cut */

keyFacts: clip-path clips an element's visible region to a shape: polygon(), circle(), ellipse(), or inset().
polygon() points are percentages of the element's own width and height, connected in order.
Clipped-away regions are transparent and do not receive pointer events — clicks pass through.
Unlike border-radius, clip-path can produce any polygonal shape: stars, arrows, chevrons, speech bubbles.
box-shadow is clipped away with the box; filter: drop-shadow() follows the clipped outline instead.
The element keeps its original rectangular layout box — clipping is visual only and does not reflow the page.
